findings.title: Sequenced version may prevent messages processing
findings.description: The version field in the update_user_account_accepted_deposit_and_claim_percentage function is implemented as a u8, which limits the maximum value to 255. This version acts as a nonce to prevent replay attacks by requiring each subsequent message to have a higher version number than the previous one. However, because the version is user-controlled and capped at 255, a user or backend error could set the version to 255 prematurely, permanently preventing further message processing for that user account. The root cause is the combination of a small integer type (u8) and lack of safeguards against misuse of the version parameter. An attacker or misconfigured frontend could exploit this by submitting a message with version 255, rendering the account unusable for future updates. The impact is limited to denial of service for a specific user account, preventing further updates to their deposit and claim settings, which could disrupt user experience but does not lead to loss of funds or critical system failure.

findings.title: The find_ed25519_instruction limits protocol’s functionality
findings.description: The find_ed25519_instruction function searches for the first instruction in the transaction that targets the ED25519 program ID and returns it. This design restricts the protocol to only process one deposit action per transaction, as it assumes the first matching instruction is the relevant one. This creates a limitation because Solana allows up to five instructions per transaction, and a common pattern is to use the preceding instruction (current_ix - 1) to locate the signature verification. By not following this pattern, the protocol loses the ability to batch multiple deposit messages in a single transaction, reducing efficiency and increasing costs for users who might want to perform multiple actions atomically. The root cause is an overly restrictive implementation of instruction parsing that does not account for common Solana best practices. While there is no direct exploit leading to fund loss or unauthorized access, the limitation reduces composability and scalability of the protocol. The impact is a missed optimization opportunity and reduced flexibility in transaction construction, which could affect user experience and gas efficiency.
